steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper asking whether large language models learn internal representations of space and time, where we probe Llama-2 and Pythia models for the real-world locations and dates of places and events. Motivate it with the world-model debate and summarize our findings.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Motivation: what do LLMs actually learn? Correlations vs. world models
- Our framing: try to extract an actual map of the world
- Datasets and probing method
- Summary of findings and paper roadmap

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Motivation
  - LLMs trained only on next-token prediction, yet impressive capabilities -> questions/concerns about what they learned
  - hypothesis 1: massive collection of correlations, no coherent model / "understanding" of data generating process (text-only training)
  - hypothesis 2: compressing data -> compact, coherent, interpretable models of generative process = world model
  - evidence: Othello transformers learn explicit board-state representations; later shown linear
  - LLMs track boolean states of subjects in context; representations reflect perceptual/conceptual structure in spatial and color domains
  - matters for robustness, fairness, safety of current and future AI
- Our framing
  - take world (and temporal) model question literally: extract an actual map of the world
  - spatiotemporal representations not a dynamic causal world model on their own
  - but coherent multi-scale space/time representations = basic ingredients of a fuller model
- Datasets and method
  - six datasets: names of places/events + space or time coordinates, multiple scales
  - space: whole world, United States, New York City
  - time: death year of historical figures (past 3000 years), release date of art/entertainment (1950s onward), publication date of news headlines (2010 to 2020)
  - Llama-2 and Pythia model families
  - linear regression probes on internal activations of the names, each layer -> latitude/longitude or numeric timestamp
- Findings / roadmap
  - representations built in early layers, plateau around halfway point; larger models consistently better (§ 3.1)
  - linear: nonlinear probes not better (§ 3.2)
  - fairly robust to prompting changes (§ 3.3)
  - unified across entity kinds (e.g. cities and natural landmarks)
  - robustness checks: generalization across data distributions (§ 4.1), probes trained on PCA components (§ 4.2)
  - individual space/time neurons + basic causal interventions -> model truly uses these features (§ 5)

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Large language models (LLMs) are trained to just predict the next token, but modern LLMs have shown an impressive set of capabilities, and this raises questions and concerns about what the models have actually learned. One hypothesis is that LLMs just learn a massive collection of correlations and don't have any coherent model or "understanding" of the data generating process underneath, since they are only trained on text. The other hypothesis is that LLMs, while compressing the data, learn more compact, coherent, and interpretable models of the generative process behind the training data, that is, a world model. For example, prior work has shown that transformers trained with next token prediction to play the board game Othello learn explicit representations of the game state, and later work showed that these representations are linear. Other work has shown that LLMs track boolean states of subjects within the context and that they have representations reflecting perceptual and conceptual structure in spatial and color domains. Understanding if and how LLMs model the world better is critical for reasoning about the robustness, fairness, and safety of current and future AI systems.

In this work we take the question of whether LLMs form world (and temporal) models as literally as we can: we try to extract an actual map of the world! These spatiotemporal representations are not a dynamic causal world model by themselves, but having coherent multi-scale representations of space and time are basic ingredients that a more comprehensive model needs.

- Datasets and method
  - six datasets, names of places/events with space or time coordinates, multiple spatiotemporal scales
  - space: whole world, United States, New York City
  - time: death year of historical figures from past 3000 years, release date of art and entertainment from 1950s onward, publication date of news headlines 2010 to 2020
  - Llama-2 and Pythia families; linear regression probes on internal activations of the names at each layer -> real-world location (latitude/longitude) or time (numeric timestamp)
- Findings / roadmap
  - built in early layers, plateau around model halfway point, larger models consistently better (§ 3.1)
  - (1) linear, nonlinear probes not better (§ 3.2); (2) fairly robust to prompting (§ 3.3); (3) unified across kinds of entities (e.g. cities and natural landmarks)
  - robustness checks: generalization across data distributions (§ 4.1), probes on PCA components (§ 4.2)
  - individual neurons activating as function of space or time; basic causal interventions verify importance -> model truly uses these features (§ 5)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Large language models (LLMs) are trained to just predict the next token, but modern LLMs have shown an impressive set of capabilities, and this raises questions and concerns about what the models have actually learned. One hypothesis is that LLMs just learn a massive collection of correlations and don't have any coherent model or "understanding" of the data generating process underneath, since they are only trained on text. The other hypothesis is that LLMs, while compressing the data, learn more compact, coherent, and interpretable models of the generative process behind the training data, that is, a world model. For example, prior work has shown that transformers trained with next token prediction to play the board game Othello learn explicit representations of the game state, and later work showed that these representations are linear. Other work has shown that LLMs track boolean states of subjects within the context and that they have representations reflecting perceptual and conceptual structure in spatial and color domains. Understanding if and how LLMs model the world better is critical for reasoning about the robustness, fairness, and safety of current and future AI systems.

In this work we take the question of whether LLMs form world (and temporal) models as literally as we can: we try to extract an actual map of the world! These spatiotemporal representations are not a dynamic causal world model by themselves, but having coherent multi-scale representations of space and time are basic ingredients that a more comprehensive model needs.

Specifically, we build six datasets that contain the names of places or events with their space or time coordinates, and they span multiple spatiotemporal scales. For space we have locations within the whole world, the United States, and New York City. For time we have the death year of historical figures from the past 3000 years, the release date of art and entertainment from 1950s onward, and the publication date of news headlines from 2010 to 2020. We use the Llama-2 and Pythia family of models and train linear regression probes on the internal activations of the names of these places and events at each layer, to predict their real-world location (i.e., latitude/longitude) or time (numeric timestamp).

The probing experiments show evidence that models build spatial and temporal representations throughout the early layers, and then the representations plateau at around the model halfway point, and larger models consistently do better than smaller ones (§ 3.1). Then we show these representations are (1) linear, because nonlinear probes do not perform better (§ 3.2), (2) fairly robust to changes in prompting (§ 3.3), and (3) unified across different kinds of entities (e.g. cities and natural landmarks). After that we do a series of robustness checks to understand how our probes generalize across different data distributions (§ 4.1) and how probes trained on the PCA components perform (§ 4.2). Last, we use our probes to find individual neurons which activate as a function of space or time, and we use basic causal interventions to verify they are important in spatiotemporal modeling, which gives strong evidence that the model is really using these features (§ 5).

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Despite being trained to just predict the next token, modern large language models (LLMs) have shown an impressive set of capabilities [1,2], raising questions and concerns about what such models have actually learned. One hypothesis is that LLMs learn a massive collection of correlations but lack any coherent model or “understanding” of the underlying data generating process, given that they only see text during training [3,4]. An alternative hypothesis is that LLMs, in the course of compressing the data, learn more compact, coherent, and interpretable models of the generative process underlying the training data, i.e., a world model. For instance, [5] have shown that transformers trained with next token prediction to play the board game Othello learn explicit representations of the game state, and [6] subsequently showed these representations are linear. Others have shown that LLMs track boolean states of subjects within the context [7] and have representations reflecting perceptual and conceptual structure in spatial and color domains [8,9]. Better understanding of if and how LLMs model the world is critical for reasoning about the robustness, fairness, and safety of current and future AI systems [10,11,12,13,14].

In this work, we take the question of whether LLMs form world (and temporal) models as literally as possible—we try to extract an actual map of the world! While such spatiotemporal representations are not a dynamic causal world model on their own, having coherent multi-scale representations of space and time are basic ingredients required in a more comprehensive model.

Specifically, we construct six datasets containing the names of places or events with corresponding space or time coordinates spanning multiple spatiotemporal scales: locations within the whole world, the United States, and New York City, as well as the death year of historical figures from the past 3000 years, the release date of art and entertainment from 1950s onward, and the publication date of news headlines from 2010 to 2020. Using the Llama-2 [15] and Pythia [16] family of models, we train linear regression probes [17,18] on the internal activations of the names of these places and events at each layer to predict their real-world location (i.e., latitude/longitude) or time (numeric timestamp).

These probing experiments show evidence that models build spatial and temporal representations throughout the early layers before plateauing at around the model halfway point, with larger models consistently outperforming smaller ones (§ 3.1). We then show these representations are (1) linear, since nonlinear probes do not perform better (§ 3.2), (2) fairly robust to changes in prompting (§ 3.3), and (3) unified across different kinds of entities (e.g. cities and natural landmarks). Next, we conduct a series of robustness checks to understand how our probes generalize across different data distributions (§ 4.1) and how probes trained on the PCA components perform (§ 4.2). Finally, we use our probes to find individual neurons which activate as a function of space or time and use basic causal interventions to verify their importance in spatiotemporal modeling, providing strong evidence that the model is really using these features (§ 5).
